questions.q: Per this lesson, is replication primarily an HA/DR mechanism?
options: No — it's a data-distribution tool; AGs and FCI are the real HA/DR mechanisms
Yes — it's SQL Server's primary failover technology
Yes — replication and Availability Groups are functionally identical
No — replication cannot copy data anywhere reliably
questions.explain: Replication exists to distribute data for reasons like reporting offload or system integration, not to provide failover.

questions.q: What does transactional replication do, per this lesson?
options: Captures changes from the transaction log and sends them to subscribers continuously, near-real-time, one direction
Takes a full copy of the data once and never updates it again
Allows changes at both the publisher and subscriber with conflict resolution
Only replicates schema, never data
questions.explain: Transactional replication is the near-real-time, one-way, log-driven workhorse type.

questions.q: What is merge replication's defining characteristic, and what's its status today per this lesson?
options: It allows bidirectional changes with conflict resolution, and it's largely a legacy/niche pattern now
It's the fastest of the three replication types and is growing in popularity
It only works with snapshot replication, never on its own
It's identical to transactional replication but with a different name
questions.explain: Merge replication supports two-way sync with conflict resolution, historically for disconnected/mobile scenarios, but it's largely legacy usage today.

questions.q: What role does snapshot replication play beyond standalone use, per this lesson?
options: It's the required initial synchronization step before transactional or merge replication can begin tracking incremental changes
It has no other purpose besides one-time reference table copies
It's required to run continuously alongside transactional replication forever
It replaces the need for a distributor
questions.explain: Snapshot replication provides the initial full copy that transactional and merge replication build their incremental tracking on top of.

questions.q: If the publisher in a transactional replication topology goes down, what happens to the subscribers, per this lesson?
options: They simply stop receiving updates — there's no built-in failover to make a subscriber take over the publisher's workload
A subscriber automatically becomes the new publisher within seconds
All subscriber databases are automatically dropped
Replication automatically converts to an Availability Group
questions.explain: Unlike an AG or FCI, replication has no built-in failover relationship — subscribers are independent databases that just stop getting updates.
